what_its_for: Levoketoconazole is used to treat adults with Cushing's syndrome, a condition where your body makes too much of a hormone called cortisol. Too much cortisol can cause weight gain, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, and other health problems. This medicine works by blocking your adrenal glands from making too much cortisol.
how_to_take: Take levoketoconazole by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or split them. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady level in your body. If you feel sick to your stomach, taking it with food may help.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how your cortisol levels respond and how well you tolerate the medicine. The usual starting dose is 150 mg taken twice a day (morning and evening). Your doctor may increase your dose every 2 to 4 weeks. The maximum dose is 600 mg twice a day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store levoketoconazole at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Store it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking grapefruit juice or eating grapefruit while taking this medicine, as it can increase the amount of drug in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid alcohol, as it can stress your liver. Do not take antacids, acid-reducing medicines (like omeprazole or famotidine), or other medicines without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist, because many drugs can interact with levoketoconazole. Avoid driving or using heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe stomach pain, or unusual tiredness — these may be signs of liver problems. Also call your doctor if you have: an irregular or fast heartbeat, fainting, severe dizziness, signs of low cortisol (extreme tiredness, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or weakness), unusual bruising or bleeding, or any new or worsening symptoms. Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting this drug.
when_it_works: It may take several weeks before your cortisol levels begin to come down. Your doctor will check your cortisol levels with blood or urine tests regularly to see how the medicine is working. You may start to notice improvements in your symptoms — such as less weight gain, better blood pressure, or improved blood sugar — over weeks to months. Keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can monitor your progress and adjust your dose if needed.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Levoketoconazole may harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment. It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk — do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Liver problems: This medicine can cause serious liver injury. Tell your doctor if you have a history of liver disease. Your liver function will be checked with blood tests before and during treatment. Kidney problems: Dose adjustments may not be needed for mild-to-moderate kidney problems, but always inform your doctor about any kidney issues. Older adults: Use with caution; older patients may be more sensitive to side effects.
